title: Heme vs. nonheme iron: differences, absorption, and food sources

seo.title: Heme vs. nonheme iron: absorption and food sources
seo.meta_description: Heme iron from meat and seafood is absorbed more efficiently; nonheme iron from plants is more affected by vitamin C, phytate and the rest of the meal.
seo.search_intent: Understand heme versus nonheme iron, where each form occurs, and why equal milligrams do not always mean equal absorption.

excerpt: Dietary iron comes mainly in heme and nonheme forms. Heme iron occurs in animal tissues and is generally absorbed more efficiently; nonheme iron occurs in plant foods, fortified foods and part of animal foods, but its absorption varies much more with the meal. That means 3 mg of iron from lentils and 3 mg from meat are not necessarily equivalent in absorbed iron. Vitamin C improves nonheme-iron absorption, while phytate and some polyphenols can reduce it.
content_html:
Two foods can list the same amount of iron and still provide the body with different amounts after digestion. The form of the iron and the rest of the meal both matter.

As a broad physiological reference, heme iron is often absorbed at roughly 15–35%, versus about 2–20% for nonheme iron; the nonheme fraction also varies more with the rest of the meal.

The two forms at a glance

Heme ironNonheme iron
Main sourcesMeat, seafood and poultryBeans, grains, nuts, seeds, vegetables and fortified foods
Approx. absorptionabout 15–35%about 2–20%, highly variable
Meal effectsSmallerLarger
Important factorsIron statusVitamin C, phytate, polyphenols, iron status and meal composition

Those percentages are broad physiological ranges, not fixed values for every meal. The body also adjusts absorption according to iron status.

Animal foods contain more than one form

Meat, poultry and seafood contain both heme and nonheme iron. Plant foods and iron-fortified products contain nonheme iron. So “animal iron versus plant iron” is a useful shortcut, but not a chemically exact one.

Why 3 mg is not always equivalent to 3 mg

Consider two meals that each contain 3 mg of iron. When a meaningful share is heme iron, the absorbed fraction is generally higher and more consistent. When all 3 mg are nonheme, the absorbed amount can shift substantially with the rest of the meal.

NIH estimates overall iron bioavailability at about 14–18% from mixed diets containing substantial meat, seafood and vitamin C, versus roughly 5–12% from vegetarian diets. That does not mean vegetarian diets cannot provide enough iron; it means bioavailability deserves more attention.

Vitamin C matters especially for plant iron

Vitamin C helps keep nonheme iron in a more soluble, absorbable form. Beans eaten with bell peppers, tomatoes, citrus or another vitamin-C-rich food therefore arrive in a different absorption environment than the same beans eaten alone.

The useful habit is not to calculate every milligram. It is to pair plant iron sources with fruits or vegetables rich in vitamin C often enough that the pattern works in your favor.

Phytate and polyphenols can pull the other way

Phytate in whole grains, legumes, nuts and seeds can bind nonheme iron and lower absorption. Some polyphenols in tea and coffee can also reduce absorption when consumed with an iron-rich meal.

That is not a reason to remove whole grains, legumes or tea from a healthy diet. Real meals contain both enhancers and inhibitors, and the body adapts absorption in response to iron status.

The practical distinction

Heme iron is more bioavailable; nonheme iron is more meal-dependent. People eating little or no animal food can still meet iron needs, but sufficient iron-rich foods and regular vitamin-C pairings become more useful.

faq.question: Which is absorbed better, heme or nonheme iron?
faq.answer: Heme iron is generally absorbed better. Broad estimates are about 15–35% for heme iron and 2–20% for nonheme iron, although iron status and meal composition can shift absorption.

faq.question: Do beans contain heme iron?
faq.answer: No. Iron in beans and other plant foods is nonheme iron.

faq.question: Does vitamin C help iron from meat?
faq.answer: Its strongest effect is on nonheme iron. Meat contains some nonheme iron too, while heme iron is less affected by the rest of the meal.
